content: Plumeria, commonly known as Frangipani, is a small genus consisting of 7-8 species that are native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. These plants are primarily deciduous shrubs and trees. One notable species, Plumeria rubra (commonly referred to as Common Frangipani or Red Frangipani), originates from Mexico, Central America, and Venezuela. Its flowers vary in color, ranging from yellow to pink, depending on the specific form or cultivar. Over time, Plumeria has spread from its native regions to tropical areas worldwide, including Hawaii, where it grows so abundantly that many mistakenly believe it to be native to the islands. Plumeria is closely related to the Oleander (Nerium oleander), and both plants produce a poisonous, milky sap similar to that of Euphorbia. Each species of Plumeria exhibits distinct leaf shapes and growth habits. For instance, the leaves of Plumeria alba are narrow and corrugated, while those of Plumeria pudica are elongated, oak-shaped, and glossy dark green. Plumeria pudica is an evergreen species that blooms continuously and does not shed its leaves. Another species, Plumeria obtusa, retains its leaves and flowers during winter. Despite its common name Singapore, Plumeria obtusa is originally from Colombia. In Eastern Africa, Plumeria is sometimes referenced in Swahili love poems. The flowers of Plumeria are most fragrant at night, a trait that helps attract sphinx moths for pollination. However, the flowers do not produce nectar and instead deceive the moths, which inadvertently transfer pollen between flowers during their futile search for nectar. Plumeria species are easily propagated by taking cuttings of leafless stem tips in the spring, allowing the cuttings to dry at the base, and then planting them in soil. They can also be propagated through tissue culture, using either freshly elongated stem cuttings or aseptically germinated seeds. The genus Plumeria, originally spelled Plumiera, was named in honor of the 17th-century French botanist Charles Plumier, who documented numerous plant and animal species in the New World. The common name Frangipani originates from an Italian noble family, one of whose members, a 16th-century marquess, created a perfume with a scent reminiscent of Plumeria. In Mexico, the plant is known by its Nahuatl (Aztec) name cacalloxochitl, meaning crow flower, and was historically used for medicinal purposes, such as in salves and ointments. Depending on the region, Plumeria is known by various other names, including Kembang Kamboja in Indonesia, Temple Tree or Champa in India, Kalachuchi in the Philippines, Araliya or Pansal Mal in Sri Lanka, Champa in Laos, and Lantom or Leelawadee in Thailand. English speakers often refer to it simply as Plumeria. Plumeria has become a naturalized plant in many parts of southern and southeastern Asia. In local folklore, it is believed to provide shelter to ghosts and demons. In Malay folklore, the scent of Plumeria is associated with the vampire-like entity known as the pontianak. The flowers are also linked to temples in Hindu and Buddhist cultures, although Hindus do not use them in temple offerings. On several Pacific islands, including Tahiti, Fiji, Hawaii, Tonga, and the Cook Islands, Plumeria is commonly used to make leis. In modern Polynesian culture, women wear Plumeria flowers to signify their relationship status—over the right ear if seeking a relationship and over the left ear if taken. Plumeria alba is the national flower of Nicaragua and Laos, where it is known as Sacuanjoche (Nicaragua) and Champa (Laos). In literature, Plumeria has been referenced in various works. In Percy Bysshe Shelley's 1819 poem Indian Serenade, the line The champak odours fail / Like sweet thoughts in a dream mentions the flower. In Joris-Karl Huysmans' 1884 novel À rebours, the persistent scent of Frangipani troubles the protagonist, Jean des Esseintes. Oscar Wilde's 1890 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray describes the lingering scent of Frangipani perfume in a room, likely referencing Huysmans. Rabindranath Tagore's 1913 story The Champa Flower, from the collection Crescent Moon, also features the flower. In Mia Couto's 1996 novel Under the Frangipani, the shedding of the tree's flowers symbolizes the passage of time, and the protagonists ultimately submerge into the tree's roots as a resolution to their fractured world. In Bangladeshi culture, white flowers, particularly Plumeria (Bengali: চম্পা, chômpa or চাঁপা, chãpa), are associated with funerals and death. Additionally, American singer-songwriter John Vanderslice referenced the Frangipani tree in his 2007 song Kookaburra from the album Emerald City.
